title: How Much Should You Save Monthly if You Want to Retire Early Without Kids?
description: The financial advantage of the 'Child-Free' lifestyle and how to leverage it for FIRE.
content:
Raising a child in the US costs over $300,000 from birth to age 18, not including college. For couples or singles who choose to remain child-free, this 'non-expense' creates a massive opportunity for wealth acceleration. Without the costs of daycare, larger housing, and 529 plans, your 'Enough' number is significantly lower, and your capacity to save is higher. This guide breaks down the math of 'DINK' (Dual Income, No Kids) or 'SINK' (Single Income, No Kids) FIRE and how fast you can exit the workforce.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Burn Rate' Advantage: Early retirement math is based on annual spending. Without kids, your spending is naturally 20-30% lower, meaning you need a smaller portfolio to retire.
  • Aggressive Savings Rate: Without childcare costs ($15k-$25k/year), a dual-income couple can realistically save 50-70% of their income, shortening the working career to 10-15 years.
  • Healthcare Flexibility: Early retirees often fear healthcare costs. Without dependents, your ACA (Obamacare) premiums are lower and your flexibility to manage income for subsidies is higher.
  • Travel as a Line Item: While you save on diapers, child-free retirees often spend more on travel. You must budget explicitly for a 'high travel' lifestyle if that is the goal.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US tax code offers Child Tax Credits, but for high earners, these phase out anyway. The financial benefit of not having dependents far outweighs the tax credits lost. Using 'Mega Backdoor Roth' strategies is often easier for child-free couples who have excess cash flow.

The Math of Freedom

Let's compare a standard family path vs. a child-free path.

The Family Path

  • Annual Spending: $100,000 (includes childcare, larger house, activities).
  • FIRE Number (25x): $2.5 Million.
  • Savings Capacity: $20,000/year.
  • Time to Retire: 35 Years.

The Child-Free Path

  • Annual Spending: $60,000 (smaller house, no kid costs).
  • FIRE Number (25x): $1.5 Million.
  • Savings Capacity: $60,000/year (redirected kid costs).
  • Time to Retire: 14 Years.

The Verdict: The decision not to have children can buy you 20 years of freedom.

Capitalizing on the Surplus

  1. Avoid 'DINK Lifestyle Creep': The trap is spending the surplus on luxury cars and fancy dinners. If you do that, you work until 65 anyway. You must save the surplus.
  2. Max All Tax Shelters: You likely have enough cash to max two 401(k)s ($46k), two Roth IRAs ($14k), and two HSAs ($8.5k). Do this every year.
  3. Smaller Housing: You don't need a 4-bedroom house in a top school district. Buying a 2-bedroom condo in a 'fun' district saves on property taxes and mortgage interest.
  4. Geo-Arbitrage: Without being tied to school calendars, you can travel or live abroad in retirement, further lowering your costs.

Frequently Asked Questions

What about Long-Term Care?

Without children to potentially help in old age, you must self-fund care. Budget for Long-Term Care Insurance or a larger 'Late Retirement' nest egg.

Is 25x spending safe?

Yes, the 4% rule holds up well. However, since your retirement might be 50+ years long, aiming for 30x spending (3.3% withdrawal rate) is safer.

Should I tell my boss?

No. Unfortunately, bias exists where bosses assume child-free people can work longer hours. Set boundaries. Work hard, but leave on time to enjoy your freedom.
